Relatedness and sex categories no longer significantly interacted (p=0.444), and the significant pairwise differences between siblings and non-siblings in mixed-sex dyads shrank markedly and were no longer significant (all p>0.60).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results from supplementary analyses.

claim: When restricting analyses to dyads with early-life familiarity, the significant pairwise differences between siblings and non-siblings in mixed-sex dyads shrank markedly and were no longer significant (all p>0.60).

claim: Much aggression specifically occurred in the context of females transferring into groups.

claim: Affiliative biases towards kin in mountain gorillas are supported at the broadest level.
source: At the broadest level, our results support the existence of affiliative biases towards kin in mountain gorillas.

claim: Gorilla social groups are tight-knit and cohesive compared to their close ape relatives.
source: First, gorilla social groups are tight-knit and cohesive compared to their close ape relatives (Goodall, 1986; Remis, 1997; Morrison et al., 2021b; Schaller and Emlen, 1963; Doran and McNeilage, 1998), reflected by remarkable features such as the ability for these groups to buffer the fitness costs of maternal loss (Morrison et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mountain gorilla groups have the ability to buffer the fitness costs of maternal loss.
source: First, gorilla social groups are tight-knit and cohesive compared to their close ape relatives (Goodall, 1986; Remis, 1997; Morrison et al., 2021b; Schaller and Emlen, 1963; Doran and McNeilage, 1998), reflected by remarkable features such as the ability for these groups to buffer the fitness costs of maternal loss (Morrison et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Morrison et al., 2021a.

claim: Ubiquitous 'play groups' of infants and juveniles frequently form around adult males in mountain gorillas.
source: Even within this tight-knit context, however, ubiquitous 'play groups' of infants and juveniles frequently form around adult males (Rosenbaum and Silk, 2022), providing similar-aged animals even more opportunities to interact and become familiar with one another.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Rosenbaum and Silk, 2022.

claim: Prosocial biases towards siblings in mountain gorillas are not fully explained by the greater familiarity that closer-in-age animals likely have.
source: Second, prosocial biases towards siblings are not fully explained by the greater familiarity that closer-in-age animals likely have (Widdig et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2003; Lynch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Biases towards kin in mountain gorillas persist even when adjusting for the frequency of mother's presence during interaction periods.
source: Finally, while mothers undoubtedly mediate social interactions of offspring, especially for immature individuals, biases towards siblings persist even when adjusting for the frequency of her presence during interaction periods.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Mountain gorillas evince much stronger maternal than paternal kin bias.
source: The observation that full and maternal siblings groomed, played, and spent more time near each other than paternal siblings or non-siblings, who tended to affiliate at comparable rates, further suggests that mountain gorillas, like several other primate species studied (Langergraber et al., 2007; Silk et al., 2006; Lynch et al., 2017), evince much stronger maternal than paternal kin bias (see also Rosenbaum et al., 2015, who found little evidence for paternal kin discrimination among fathers and offspring).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The asymmetric bias in affiliation persists even though the high reproductive skew of mountain gorillas opposes the dynamic thought to underlie such biases in other primate species.
source: Interestingly, this 'asymmetric bias' in affiliation seems to persist even though the high reproductive skew of mountain gorillas opposes the dynamic thought to underlie such biases in other primate species (i.e. low reproductive skew; Galezo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results and supported by citation to Galezo et al., 2022.

claim: Single-male gorilla groups across research sites are genetically polygynous.
source: Current evidence indicates that single-male gorilla groups across research sites are genetically polygynous (reviewed in Rosenbaum and Silk, 2022), and while there can be considerable temporal variation, reproductive skew is generally much higher in multi-male gorilla groups than in, for example, chimpanzee, savannah baboon, or rhesus macaque groups (Vigilant et al., 2015; Surbeck et al., 2017; Alberts et al., 2003; Widdig et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Reproductive skew is generally much higher in multi-male gorilla groups than in chimpanzee, savannah baboon, or rhesus macaque groups.
source: Current evidence indicates that single-male gorilla groups across research sites are genetically polygynous (reviewed in Rosenbaum and Silk, 2022), and while there can be considerable temporal variation, reproductive skew is generally much higher in multi-male gorilla groups than in, for example, chimpanzee, savannah baboon, or rhesus macaque groups (Vigilant et al., 2015; Surbeck et al., 2017; Alberts et al., 2003; Widdig et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to Vigilant et al., 2015; Surbeck et al., 2017; Alberts et al., 2003; Widdig et al., 2004.

claim: Mountain gorillas exhibit a comparable maternal sibling bias to other primate species due to a mismatch between their historical mating structure and their contemporary social structure.
source: We propose that, despite possessing a mating system quite unlike these other primate species, mountain gorillas still exhibit a comparable maternal sibling bias due to a mismatch between their historical mating structure–which we infer consisted of highly polygynous one-male units–and their contemporary social structure of tight-knit, often multi-male groups.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in the discussion based on the results.

claim: The historical mating structure of mountain gorillas consisted of highly polygynous one-male units.
source: We propose that, despite possessing a mating system quite unlike these other primate species, mountain gorillas still exhibit a comparable maternal sibling bias due to a mismatch between their historical mating structure–which we infer consisted of highly polygynous one-male units–and their contemporary social structure of tight-knit, often multi-male groups.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the discussion.

claim: If co-residency was enough to identify paternal kin with reasonable accuracy, a more sophisticated recognition mechanism would be unlikely to evolve.
source: In other words, while individuals in highly polygynandgrous groups might find it too difficult to detect and adjust affiliation toward paternal kin, perhaps mountain gorillas fail to do so because, until very recently, it was unnecessary. If co-residency was enough to identify paternal kin with reasonable accuracy, a more sophisticated recognition mechanism would be unlikely to evolve.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion.

claim: The study had far less information about sibling relationships in single-male groups than in multi-male groups.
source: One important limitation of our analyses is that we have far less information about sibling relationships in single-male groups—where shared paternity is nearly or entirely certain—than we do about siblings in multi-male groups, where reproductive skew is high but not 100%.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a limitation of the study.

claim: Patterns of aggressive behavior suggest there may be kin recognition mechanisms at play for all sibling types in mountain gorillas.
source: Notably, while we see little evidence that mountain gorillas show a prosocial bias towards paternal siblings, patterns of aggressive behavior suggest there may still be kin recognition mechanisms at play for all sibling types.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Aggression remained low across most combinations of relatedness and sex configurations, with one exception: mixed-sex interactions among non-siblings.

claim: Traditional mechanistic explanations for sibling biases that appeal to exposure during developmental periods appear largely inconsistent with the results and the nature of mountain gorilla sociality.
source: First, traditional mechanistic explanations for sibling biases that typically appeal to exposure during developmental periods appear largely inconsistent with our results and the nature of mountain gorilla sociality, in which siblings and non-siblings, and maternal and paternal siblings, are all likely to have significant exposure to one another during development.

source: Given low incidences of many behaviors, we aggregated behaviors into annual counts, making the dyad-year the fundamental unit of analysis (total n=7832).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Counts of contact and non-contact aggression were summed into a single category for analysis.
source: Even with annual aggregation, instances of aggression were uncommon. Therefore, counts of contact and non-contact aggression were summed into a single category for analysis (see Appendix 4—figures 1 and 2; Appendix 4—Tables 1 and 2 for results with individual aggression categories, which were qualitatively similar to those reported below).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The study included the proportion of observations with mothers in close proximity as a covariate in all models.
source: As mothers plausibly mediate many of the social behaviors we examined, especially early in life, we also included the proportion of observations with mothers in close proximity (i.e. the average proportion between the two members of the dyad for that observation year), and this variable's interaction with relatedness, as covariates in all models.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The study did not include the natal group structure of the dyad due to the small number of dyads available in single-male groups.
source: We did not include the natal group structure of the dyad (i.e. single versus multi-male) due to the small number of dyads we had available in which both individuals grew up single-male groups (n=10 dyads, 60 dyad-years), and due to the lack of variability of relatedness–all dyads in these groups were paternal siblings.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section as a methodological decision.

claim: The study modeled count outcomes as rates with a negative binomial family and an offset term for exposure time.
source: We modeled our count outcomes as rates with a negative binomial family in glmmTMB and an offset term for exposure time (either logged hours of observation, or logged sum of scans for both individuals, per dyad-year).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: All data and code necessary to reproduce the results are available publicly at https://osf.io/6qgj5.
source: All data and code necessary to reproduce our results are available publicly at https://osf.io/6qgj5.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.
